item.title: New Makita Maktrak Drawer Tool Boxes are Shockingly Boring
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: I expected different.
item.content:encoded:
Several online retailers launched presale pages for 2 new Makita Maktrak drawer tool boxes.

Shown above is the Makita Maktrak 3-drawer tool box, T-90118.

There are also listings for a 2-drawer Maktrak tool box, T-90102.

The descriptions mention a 50 lb capacity and padlock loop.

If these are accurate depictions, and not just placeholder images, well, they look just fine.

Most modern pro-grade modular tool box systems feature external accessory attachment points, and we’re seeing similar on many DIY and consumer-grade storage systems. I don’t see any external accessory rails on either of the new Makita drawer tool boxes.

Where’s the innovation here? This is it?

Maybe there are some special features that aren’t obvious yet.

Boring isn’t necessarily bad. I just expected more. The designs look ordinary and maybe even forgettable. I guess that’s what users wanted?

The Maktrak platform is just 2 years old. Makita is just getting started – there’s plenty of time for more innovation to come.

The 2-drawer tool box is listed at $249, and the 3-drawer at $279.

Update: As Jake pointed out in the comments, the pricing is likely CAD. So that would be ~$178 USD for the 2-drawer, and ~$199 USD for the 3-drawer.

For comparison, the Milwaukee Packout 2-drawer tool box is $179 at Home Depot at the time of this posting, and the Packout 3-drawer tool box is $199.

item.title: New Photos of Bambu H3C and P3C 3D Printers with Tool Changers
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: Here's a look at Bambu's new 3D printers.
item.content:encoded:
Here are new photos of the upcoming Bambu H3C and P3C tool-changing 3D printers.

Bambu recently published a teaser of their new H3C 3D printer, but so far the P3C has only been revealed in regulatory filings.

From the images, the Bambu H3C is a 9-nozzle 3D printer, and the P3C will be a 7-nozzle 3D printer.

See Also:

  • Bambu Announced their Black Friday 2026 3D Printer Deals
  • Shop Bambu Black Friday Deals
  • Bambu H3C 3D Printer is About to Launch
  • Snapmaker U1 4-Head 3D Printer – New Low price at Amazon
  • Creality K3 Multi-Material Multi-Color Printer Preorder

Bambu P3C 3D Printer

The Bambu P3C looks to maintain the same format as their P2S and X2D 3D printers.

Here we can see 7 tool heads. It’s possible the Bambu P3C tool heads will be interchangeable with the H3C tool heads.

Interestingly, this is designated P3C. Does that mean an X2C or X3C model will also be in the works?

This a view of the Bambu P3C 3D printer from above, which all but confirms that the tool changer will be positioned at the very front of the machine.

There’s not much to see on the left side of the Bambu P3C.

Or the right side.

Here’s the rear – also showing the 7 nozzle tool changing system at the front of the Bambu P3C 3D printer.

Here’s a view of the bottom.

Bambu H3C 3D Printer

As expected, the Bambu H3C looks to maintain the same larger format sizing of the H2 series.

The Bambu H3C’s tool changing system is also placed at the front of the machine.

Looking at the inside, the Bambu H3C has a single tool head carrier.

The changing system is also positioned at the front end of the H3C.

There’s not much on either side of the H3C printer, aside from windows towards the top.

Here’s the rear of the H3C.

And the bottom.

More details should be availble soon.

We also haven’t seen what the new Bambu AMS or filament holding system will look like. Their existing AMS 2 filament changing system has a single output. These new Bambu 3D printers have 7-tool and 9-tool head systems. This will support simultaneous loading that requires a different setup.

Bambu is announcing the H3C 3D printer launch on November 3, 2026. They have not yet teased the P3C 3D printer announcement yet.

Compare to Snapmaker U1 at Amazon

Source: FCCID.io Database with Japan Giteki Testing Documents

item.title: I Have Been Using AI for a Creative Maker Project
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: This has been interesting for me to explore.
item.content:encoded:
I recently started using Google’s Gemini AI image generation tool for maker-type creative projects.

My son is doing something different for Halloween this year. He’s been playing Fallout 4, and wanted a costume that ties into that. DIY power armor. That’s not happening in the time frame we gave ourselves.

Character with chest piece painted with Enclave (game faction) decor, and some accents that build up a wasteland wanderer appearance? That I can do.

I tried to order a cheap motorcycle chest protector from Amazon. It was delayed and it seems. They lost it. We’ll be going with foam and craft materials, maybe I’ll talk about that more later.

I have been focusing my attention on the props. A Milwaukee black hard hat should suffice for head gear, and we’ll duct-tape a cheap flashlight for that “scavenged and put it to use” look.

Since we’re not going heavy with crafted power armor, the prop has to “pop.”

I can visualize some of the elements, but not quite enough to run through the modeling.

I am competent when it comes to modeling things I’ve modeled before. See How I 3D-Modeled My Small Box Test Part.

But when it comes to modeling new things? That’s more of a challenge.

It’s so much more difficult when I’m trying to model a part that I have not fully conceptualized. I think that’s where the AI comes in.

I sought to model a truncated cone with a mounting ring.

It took a bunch of iterations, but I eventually settled on how to approach it – 2 connected truncated cones.

Google provided OpenSCAD code. Other AI services could probably create the entire 3D model, but the OpenSCAD code worked for me.

The code also let me change parameters until I was happy with the geometry and dimensions.

The print – with very wet filament (I’m drying it right now) – is good enough to help me move to the next stage.

The next revision will be a little larger, and the top part of the cone with have mounting holes so I can screw it to a wooden box that I’ll build as the main component for the prop.

As an aside, the green parts are non-pressurizable air fittings printed using McMaster Carr 3D files, so that I can visualize how they would integrate into the assembly with 1/4″ ID (inner diameter) air hoses. I haven’t decided if I will go with inexpensive metal fittings, and used this as a way to ensure I didn’t over-order an excessive variety since I rarely use barbed fittings.

I need a handle.

The AI made a lot of mistakes, and I’m also learning how to better constrain dimensions in my prompts.

Here, the AI ignored the directive to have the side arms flush, and also ignored the directive to have the pill-shaped holes in just the main face. It also created large undesirable chamfers.

On the bright side, this helped me visualize things in three dimensional space before modeling.

I might not need to model it manually – after much prompting (Gemini Pro gave me a timeout and dropped me to the lower AI tier until the clock reset) the OpenSCAD code provided a usable model.

I modified some of the parameters in the code, adding more holes in the mounting plate and changing the dimensions of the slots in the vertical columns.

I’m printing a low density version of this right now. If it works, I’ll print it in the final color, probably black, or remodel in Fusion or similar so that I can have easier control over different dimensions and their dependenacies.

Just now I tried to get Gemini to breakdown the fantasy tool into 3D-printable subassembly components. Shown here is the tool from various Wikis.

I doubt anyone will recognize that, not to mention it looks very difficult to make, which is why I convinced my son to let me take a more creative approach to design a prop from scratch.

I’m trying to convince him to go with a synth, ghoul, or mutant detector. The current plan is to build the prop together, and then he’ll call it whatever he wants.

This is the rear view.

Here’s what the Gemini AI gave me as a simplified breakdown of subassemblies. That’s not very helpful, but it does validate my previous idea to have mounting pins for glue-on assembly.

My vision for the prop still lives entirely in my head. That’s a big part of the challenge.

For example, my son wants wires on the outside, and I have ideas on how to do that. But translating a mental image into a model and then a model that can be turned into an actual part – that’s always been difficult for me.

One part? Easy. Multiple parts? A little more difficult. Multiple parts that all assemble together? That’s where I get lost in planning and eventually use hardware, hot glue, epoxy, or similar to combine things.

Cohesive design is something I’ll work on more.

In the meantime, here’s the handle mid-print.

I will probably remodel the handle in Fusion or similar software – manually, as that would more easily enable me to make quick changes, big or small, for this or future projects.

If I remodel everything in 3D software, rather than OpenSCAD, I should be able to work on the cohesive assembly aspect. But probably not for this project. My current plan here is to screw or glue a bunch of individually designed and modeled parts to a small wood box, maybe the size of a tissue box.

It’s not the ideal approach, but will let me integrate as many creative components and maybe functions as possible. Some hot glue might be involved. Because time is running out.

I’m having fun. Nothing looks elegant yet. There’s so much work ahead.

The current plan is to create a rough V1 prop so that we have something, and I’ll then refine things – hopefully in time for Halloween.

I took a chance using AI, but as a tool it’s definitely helping me with some of the tedious steps I typically struggle with.

item.title: Bambu Announced their Black Friday 2026 3D Printer Deals
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: Bambu announced their sale pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Bambu Labs has announced Black Friday 2026 deal pricing on their full range of desktop 3D printers. The sale starts October 27, 2026 and is said to end on December 1st.

These are the Bambu 3D printer deals I’d pay the most attention to:

  • X2D Combo (Dual-Nozzle 3D Printer for Everyone – $789 (was $899)
  • P2S Combo (All-Round Best Value Workhorse) – $649 (was $749)
    • Check the P2S Price at Amazon
  • H2C Combo (Specialized for Multi-Material Printing) – $1899 (was $2199)
  • H2S Combo (Ultimate Single-Nozzle 3D Printer) – $1249 (was $1399)

Here are additional deals:

  • H2D AMS Combo (Personal Manufacturing Hub) – $1599 (was $1749)
  • P1S Combo (Proven Reliability) – $509 (was $579) – OLD MODEL
    • Check the P1S Price at Amazon
  • A1 Combo (Simple for Beginners) – $359 (was $399)
  • A1 Mini (Most Affordable Entry) – $199 (was $219)
  • A2L (Most Accessible Mega-Size Printer) – $519 (was $569)

Bambu will also have 3D printing filament deals – mainly bulk order discounts on PLA and PETG, similar to the promos they hold throughout the year – discounts on spare parts, Maker’s Supply project parts, build plates, and other accessories or components.

Buy Bambu Black Friday Deals

I have seen some Bambu 3D printer deals extend into and beyond December in past years, but there’s no guarantee that will happen.

The most popular 3D printers and combos sometimes sell out early, but I have also seen restocks and reasonable backorder shipping ETAs.

In other words, shop early if you’re in a rush, but you probably don’t have to.

Looking at the pricing, Bambu is offering substantial discounts on their 3D printers.

These are the lowest prices I’ve seen on a lot of their 3D printers, including the H2C that was just $2399 a few months ago, and the X2D that launched at $899 earlier this year.

The “was” pricing in the links above were taken from the live store pages on 10/22, ahead of the Black Friday deal pricing activation on 10/27/26.

Here are my quick notes and opinions for those starting on their 3D printer buying journey:

Bambu Labs 3D Printers I Would Buy

X2D – flagship compact printer, second nozzle is really only for support materials (but that’s still a great selling point).

P2S – lower-priced option that’s missing some of the X2D’s good-to-have features.

H2C – (former?) flagship larger printer with nozzle changer on one side, cuts down on waste, but is mainly a big convenience for multiple materials or nozzle sizes without having to make changes between prints.

See Also: Bambu H3C 3D Printer is About to Launch
Also Consider: Snapmaker U1 via Amazon
Also Consider: Prusa Core One Gen 2 with INDX 8-Tool Changer

H2S – larger single nozzle printer at lower cost than the H2D and H2C. You can still use multiple materials or colors, as the combo comes with an AMS filament changer, just with a lot of waste as it purges the nozzle between changes.

Bambu Labs 3D Printers I Would NOT Buy

There are reasons to buy these 3D printers, but I think they are most suitable for users who have specific preferences.

H2D – larger dual nozzle printer, more expensive than the H2S, simpler than the H2C but not quite as convenient.

P1S – older model at lower price than the P2S. Money saved now vs “I wish I had the newer features and tech” sentiments later.

A1, A1 Mini, A2L – open frame models for users where lower cost is the highest priority. These would get destroyed in my workshop setting. The A1 Mini might be a good pick for someone who wants a 3D printer but isn’t convinced they’ll do much or stick with it.

Buy Bambu Black Friday Deals

item.title: Bambu H3C 3D Printer is About to Launch
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: It looks like a new model is about to launch.
item.content:encoded:
There have been rumors of a new Bambu Lab H3C tool changing 3D printer, starting with an FCC license registration last month.

Today, a Redditor (or Bambu plant) reported seeing a teaser on Bambu’s Australian store front, setting November 4th as the unveiling date. The banner has since been taken down.

See Also: Bambu Announced their Black Friday 2026 3D Printer Deals

Update: Bambu set 9am EST on November 3rd, 2026,as the official announcement time for the new H3C “gamer changer” 9-head “tool changer” 3D printer.

While I’ve seen plenty of AI renderings and examples of what the Bambu H3C could look like, there’s evidence this was a legit photo that was dimmed for Bambu’s teaser.

A number of 3D printing enthusiasts have suggested that Bambu has intentionally leaked the H3C teaser to drive up interest. If so, it certainly seems to have worked. (More on this at the end of the post.)

It looks like the Bambu H3C will feature a 9 printhead tool changer.

I bought a Bambu H2C earlier this year. It’s a bit janky compared to my X1C, and definitely feels a bit rushed to market and improvised.

I’m not saying that you shouldn’t buy the H2C, but if I were in the market for a Bambu 3D printer or a tool-changing 3D printer, I would hold off right now until Bambu makes their next announcement.

Bambu likes to tease products, then announce them, and then launch them.

If the November 4th ETA is accurate for the Bambu H3C announcement, we’ll see a fuller picture in just under 2 weeks.

Meanwhile, it looks like Snapmaker settled on a new low price for their U1 4-toolhead 3D Printer. The U1 was an $800 Kickstarter, retailed for $849, and is now $749.

Buy the Snapmaker at Amazon

I highly doubt that the Bambu H3C will be anywhere close to this price. But if we’re on the cusp of another new launch, it’s best to hold off until then. Maybe they’ll lower the price of the H2C. It’s also possible the H3C will be replacing the H2C.

Buy the H2C via Bambu

In related news, there has been controversy over the Bondtech nozzles used in the Prusa-compatible INDX system. It was advertised that the system would feature hardened nozzles, but manufacturing difficulties resulted in the tool changing system shipping with less durable nozzles.

There’s been accusations of “bait and switch,” and customers were offered apologies and compensation packages to make up for it.

See Prusa 3D Printers

Creality teased about their new KliTek nozzle-changing 3D printer nearly 5 months ago, but hasn’t revealed much since then. See Creality Announces KliTek 3D Printer Nozzle Changing.

I expect there to be quite a few announcements over the next 2 months as we enter a very busy holiday shopping season.

With promotional pricing and deal bundles on the horizon, I probably wouldn’t buy any 3D printer right now.

But with the H3C apparently about to be announced, I wouldn’t make up my mind about higher-priced tool-changing or multi-color 3D printers just yet.

Credit: u/Equivalent-Visit-560 via Sorry bambu, I have the screen shot of H3C now… at Reddit

Interestingly, the Redditor who posted the screen capture has near-zero post history aside from sharing this screen capture and 1 comment from 4 years ago.

In their comment from 4 years ago, the only public activity that preceded their sharing about the Bambu H3C, the same Redditor posted a sales email address connected to a plastics enclosure manufacturing company based in Shenzhen, China, and Whatsapp phone number with mainland China area code.

They could be a 3D printing enthusiast in Australia (as they say), or somehow connected to Bambu Labs, which is based in Shenzhen, China.

This could very well be a secret attempt by Bambu to create buzz ahead of the “official” launch.

Or maybe this person who sold plastic and aluminum enclosures for a Chinese company moved to Australia and became a 3D printing enthusiast.

I don’t think the context changes anything, I just found it interesting.

item.title: Klein Tools is Entering the Wire Nut and Connector Industry
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: This came as a surprise!
item.content:encoded:
Klein Tools is now making electrical wire connectors, starting with twist-on wire nuts.

A reader wrote in (thanks Abe!), saying:

Klein wire nuts?

Klein is now in the wire nut industry? And who did they get the patent from?

Klein wire nuts? What are you talking about? Oh.

A quick search and yes, Klein Tools now has wire nuts.

They all seem to be the winged twist-on-kind.

Different color-coded sizes.

Skirted wire nuts too.

Marketing images show that they can be installed with ordinary nut drivers.

But you can also twist them on.

There are 4 sizes, sold in various bulk packs and assortments.

Here’s the size chart for the winged connectors.

Skirted connectors are available in 2 sizes.

Here’s the size chart for the skirted connectors.

The hex drive tops, allowing nut drivers and other such tools to be used, could be a big selling point.

There are some wire nut installation tools, such as the Ideal Spin-Twist but they’re proprietary and require carrying an additional specialty driver tool in your tool pouch or bag.

So far there’s no information about where the new Klein Tools wiring connectors will be sold.

Do you think that they’ll stop here? Or will Klein start offering more types of wire connectors and electrical installation components?

Ideal has been a popular go-to wire nut brand for a while. Do you think that Lowe’s is going to stock Klein wire nuts alongside Ideal’s, or instead of them?

Thank you Abe for the heads-up!

item.title: Smaller Makita MakTrak Tool Boxes are Launching in USA
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: More new Maktrak.
item.content:encoded:
According to recent influencer reports, new Makita Maktrak tool boxes are confirmed to be launching in the USA in time for the holiday shopping seasons.

This major second wave expansion of compact MakTrak products follows 2 years after Maktrak first launched in the USA.

I was at my local Home Depot this week, and found the entire line of full-size Makita Maktrak tool boxes covered in a thick layer of dust.

The “fits in your pickup truck” concept makes sense, and the engineering was excellent. But perhaps the USA market is more welcoming to a more “standard” form factor.

More options is always good news.

I previously posted about the new rolling tool box and rolling drawer tool box – Makita Launched New MakTrak Rolling Tool Boxes, plus a smaller-size accessory box.

It looks like Makita is further expanding their compact wave 2 Maktrak tool box products with new open-top crates in shallow and deep sizes.

There have been photos online that some of the new Makita MakTrak tool boxes are made in China. This could just be for certain regions and they’re employing a “make it near where you sell it” strategy.

Makita has not yet said whether the new Maktrak products that are launching in the USA are made here or if they’re imported. I presume that the new products will continue to be made here, but we’ll see.

I also haven’t seen any drawer tool boxes aside from the new roller base unit. Maybe drawer tool boxes will arrive with the next wave of new Maktrak launches.

Buy Maktrak via Acme Tools

item.title: Bosch Officially Entered the Hand Tool Industry
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: Big news from Bosch.
item.content:encoded:
With very bold messaging, Bosch has announced that they’re entering the hand tool industry.

Bosch has had a very limited selection of hand tools for many years now, but it never seemed like a full or committed effort.

They started with utility knives, which eventually made their way to USA stores.

They launched pliers in Europe around 2.5 years ago.

At the same time they launched a limited selection of insulated pliers. (See New Bosch Tools – Cordless Nailers, Wrenches, Pliers, More.)

The utility knives landed in the USA at Amazon, and then Lowe’s (See Bosch Utility Knives are Now at Lowe’s.)

But now, it seems they’re going all-in, with screwdrivers, hammers, adjustable wrenches, saws, pliers, and even more. In their teaser image, I also spy combination wrenches and a carpentry-type mechanical pencil with lead refills.

It seems that Bosch has pulled out all the stops and is surging forward with hand tools in a big way.

This looks to be a proper entrance, rather than a limited toes-in-the-water experiment.

I asked “what if Bosch made hand tools?” in a post 11.5 years ago – What if Bosch Made Hand Tools?. The landscape is very different now, for Bosch as a tool brand and broader company, and the same is true about the USA tool market.

I think there’s an opening for Bosch hand tools at Lowe’s, alongside Klein as a pro hand tool brand offering. There could also be a small opening for Klein to launch cordless power tools at Lowe’s, but that’s a discussion for another time.

That’s still what it would take to gain traction in the USA in a reasonable length of time – in-store placement and visibility, rather than just some SKUs listed at online retailers.

Here’s another teaser image, which Bosch is using as a thumbnail with an overlayed title “are these the last hand tools you’ll ever buy?”

It’s as if someone told Bosch “go big or go home” and they said “okay, we’ll go BIG!”

So, when are these tools coming to the USA? And when are the tools coming to Lowe’s and online dealers? I’ll post updates if or when I learn more.

item.title: New Craftsman Limited Edition Tool Set Advent Calendar
item.dc:creator: Stuart

item.content:encoded:
Craftsman has launched a Advent Calendar for the 2026 holiday season, packed with tools and “products designed to delight all kinds of DIYers.”

They’re saying this is a limited edition release – “grab this exclusive product while you can (and before it’s gone for good!)”

There’s a “hidden reward,” – a “bonus deal on a future Craftsman purchase.” I figure that’s a coupon of some sort.

It took some digging, but I found a list of tools included in the Craftsman CMMT12426A advent calendar:

item.title: AI Should be a Cautious Choice
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: Let's talk about AI again.
item.content:encoded:
I have been inundated with ads featuring Meta/Facebook’s new Muse AI assistant.

“Muse organizes your inbox.”

No. I’m not giving [another] big corporate tech company access to my email inbox. I’ve already heard some horror stories about Meta’s Muse AI bungling things, such as by arranging in-person pickups for sales that aren’t possible.

I guess the new Meta AI explains why Meta has been scraping ToolGuyd data for the past few months – I was wondering what they were trying to train. I blocked their bots at some point.

AI agents are still very much training on the prompts and data you feed it. This is something people don’t realize.

“Let me run that through Claude/Chat GPT/Muse/etc.” Would you be fine with competitors listening in on the conversation? Looking at the presentation over your shoulder?

In many cases, whatever you do with an AI becomes part of it.

Moving on, let’s talk about Google AI Overview, which has been decimating traffic numbers for online publishers.

I was at Home Depot yesterday, doing a store-walk ahead of the holiday deals season to scope things out. I also had a $10 off $75 coupon code that I was using on supplies, but I wasn’t at the threshold yet.

I’m due some time for myself, and will be taking day to really test out the Traeger smoker that arrived a few weeks ago (thanks, Home Depot), and some other food-related things. (It wasn’t a test sample, it was part of Home Depot’s creator event gift package, so there was no rush.)

I need pellets, but didn’t do my research ahead of time. I had planned on researching and buying wood pellets, but happened to be at the store before I could do all that.

Home Depot had a 20 pound bag of Traeger Signature Blend pellets, with a mix of maple, cherry, and hickory. $20.

Next to it was a stack of Traeger Pro Blend wood pellets in 30 pound bags, with a mix of oak, hickory, and cherry. $25.

There were other bags, presumably specific mixes, but they were blocked off.

What’s the difference, aside for $25 for 30 pounds being a better value than $20 for 20 pounds?

Let me Google that.

Traeger does not make a product called “Pro Blend – the comparison is typically between Traeger Signature Blend pellets and other all-purpose blends like Pit Boss Competition Blend or Costco’s Kirkland Signature Blend.

I was staring at a bag or Traeger Pro Blend that Google’s AI Overview insisted didn’t exist.

It’s mid-late October and past the end of grilling season (at least for retailers). Even if this was a new offering, it would have been on the market for at least several months.

Something obviously went wrong. Every query had the same result, with Google AI refusing to acknowledge that this bag of Traeger Pro Blend existed.

Earlier in the day, I kept trying to compare compact LED lights – the Aputure MC which retails between $76 and $90, and the Smallrig RM120 and then the Amaran Ace 25C. No matter how I modified the prompt, even adding “non-pro”, Google’s AI kept referring to the $179-$199 Aputure MC Pro, which is a completely different product with larger form factor.

The AI kept pushing comparisons that I didn’t care for, rather than the ones I wanted it to make.

AI works kind of alright when it does, and completely fails when it doesn’t.

The answers, as with the Traeger pellets, sound confident without necessarily being helpful.

I grabbed the Signature Blend, as a Home Depot worker wanted to shut down the aisle to move some pallets around with heavy machinery, and I didn’t want to keep them waiting. Maybe I’ll try the Pro Blend after I burn through all these pellets. Next, I need a dry container to keep the pellets in.

Let’s talk about AI emails. I’ve been getting a lot of those, but one that I received yesterday was very different.

The phrase “outside-reference question” suggests they want me to link to their site in a post.

I regularly receive a lot of random “can we buy a link” and “can we pay you to publish our guest posts” types of requests from SEO “experts.” The idea is that links tell Google “hey, this stuff is good,” and it boosts the referenced website in search results. I just ignore them.

They referenced my Bosch laser distance measuring tool deal post from Prime Day – My Favorite Bosch Laser Distance Measuring Tool is on Sale for Prime Day. I guess that’s where they wanted a link insertion.

The email has a co-signature naming an individual and Synapse AI. They also say the email was prepared with Codex, another AI service.

I actually think that’s a good way to approach things, acknowledging that an AI was partly or perhaps mostly behind an email.

So, this was an AI-crafted or distributed email.

It referenced an article – a “guide” that the email says was “AI-assisted.”

The entire article was about whether this company’s laser pointer can measure distance, which it cannot.

It talks about Leica laser distance measuring tools, has some unintuitive language about reference points and accuracy, and briefly discusses about how pointing a laser at something doesn’t give you a measurement.

Does a laser pointer company really need AI-generated articles about how “can laser pointers measure distance?”

Just saying “no” would save so many words.

It’s a laser pointer company, and so all of this talk about checking with measurements start, and accuracy specs are moot.

Maybe it’s like how Amazon and other retailers will bid on sponsored shopping keywords for brands and products they don’t sell, just to get you through the digital door?

Or maybe an AI-generated marketing plan was fed into a separate AI that generated the “article”, and that all fed into another AI that crafted and sent the email to an AI-generated and curated list.

The email wasn’t actually clear on what they wanted from me. Did they want a link to the nonsensical “field guide”? Or mention of their laser pointer product?

People are increasingly letting AI make decisions for them. AI services lack feelings, emotions, and thinking. It’s just pattern recognition, aggregation, and recall.

I used AI the other day to check some new coding, and then also to mock-up an image of how a part for an upcoming project could look. It worked great for that, saving me time. But I’m not deferring to AI, I’m using it as a tool.

I’ve been asking questions related to strength-building, to double-check the rationale behind rep and set patterns. Consolidated opinions are helpful, as are pros and counterpoints, and the summaries quickly informed and nudged my decision-making.

Sometimes when I’m researching two products, AI will provide conflicting guidance depending on the prompt.

I have been trying to leverage AI without deferring to its judgement. Meanwhile, I have been hearing about people feeding their entire businesses through AI.

How do you trust decision-making to unfeeling algorithms that get so much wrong?

It’s like using a stud finder without caution. If you see a drywall seam, and an electrical box, there’s likely a stud. If a stud finder tells you there isn’t a stud there, are you going to believe it? Many people might not look for or recognize the drywall seam or the outlet box, and just implicitly listen to the stud finder. It seems that’s the kind of thing happening with AI.

AI services are increasingly being treated not as tools but as substitutes for critical thinking and thoughtful decision-making.

Just… be careful.

item.title: New Husky Pliers are a Hard No for Me
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: I'm not a fan of this type of pliers.
item.content:encoded:
Home Depot just launched new compound action high leverage pliers, and they’re all a hard “NO” for me.

Nevermind that I have tons of pliers, there’s always room for more. Just not these.

The new pliers line includes:

  • 8-inch linesman pliers
  • 8.5-inch long nose pliers
  • 7.5-inch diagonal cutting pliers

I’m sure they’re fine and on-par with what one can expect from pliers that are priced at $13 each.

With the new compound action high leverage pliers, Home Depot says you get 50% easier cutting compared to comparable to “standard” pliers.

It’s not exactly apples to apples, as the product descriptions compare the 7.5-inch diagonal cutting pliers to “7-inch standard diagonal pliers,” and the 8.5-inch long nose pliers to “8-inch standard diagonal pliers.”

I am sure that the claim is reasonably accurate.

But I can’t stand the compromise, with rare exceptions.

Single-action compound leverage pliers basically trade cutting effort for handle spread.

Wider handle spread means you can forget about working in tighter spaces or gripping larger parts.

I’ve got medium-sized hands. Maybe I’m more sensitive to the discomfort of having to squeeze a wider handle, but your hand size or comfort level won’t help wide-open pliers fit into smaller spaces.

And it’s not just smaller spaces, but electrical cabinets, boxes, enclosures, or any area where there are obstructions or parts nearby.

I have a great pair of high-leverage cutting pliers, and I use them only when needed. Otherwise, it’s so much more comfortable for me to just use standard cutting pliers.

Yes, they take more pressure, but it’s easier for me to apply that pressure to narrow-spread pliers than to apply less pressure to wider-spread pliers.

I’d rather opt for longer standard-design tools, such as 9.5-inch linesman pliers or 9-inch diagonal cutters, which deliver higher cutting power due to the longer handle length.

Are there advantages? Yes. For me, they’re not worth the compromise. I feel very strongly against this style of pliers.

Buy the Lineman at Home Depot
Buy the Diagonal at Home Depot
Buy the Long Nose at Home Depot

The Rare Exception

I love my NWS Fantastico pliers for harder cuts. It doesn’t seem to open as wide, but I also haven’t made direct comparisons. The high-end quality tier could also influence the experience.

But despite my fondness for NWS and their high-leverage cutters, I only bring it out for specific applications or when I start struggling or fatiguing with other tools.

See also: Knipex vs NWS Pliers – Which Brand Makes the Best Pliers?

It looks like the price came down over the years, or maybe it’s temporary. The rebranded Felo pliers cost a lot more.

item.title: Lowe’s FREE Dewalt Cordless Power Tool Deal is Live (Black Friday 2026)
item.dc:creator: Stuart
item.description: It looks like the Black Friday deal season has begun.
item.content:encoded:
Several FREE Dewalt cordless power tool deals just went live at Lowe’s.

Lowe’s kicked off their holiday promotional campaign this week, inviting shoppers to “get Christmas gifts for DIY enthusiasts…” and so forth.

I thought that was odd, since Halloween is still more than 2 weeks away.

Acme Tools listed a new Dewalt 20V Max starter kit. It’s not yet available. October launches like that tend to foreshadow holiday promotions. So I grabbed the model number and started searching.

To my surprise, I found 3 new deals at Lowe’s, which the retailer says ends 1/20/27.

Buy the Dewalt 20V cordless power tool starter kit with a 4Ah battery and 8Ah Powerpack battery, and you get 2 FREE tools.

Buy this other Dewalt starter kit with 2x 5Ah batteries, and you get 1 FREE tool.

Buy this starter kit, with faster charger and 2x 8Ah XR Powerpack tabless cell batteries, and you get 3 FREE tools.

The 2-free tool deal will cost you $299, and the same is true at this time for the 1-free tool deal. I’m guessing that the 1-free tool promo will drop to $199 at some point, otherwise who’s going to spend the same money for far less value?

The 3-free tool deal is $449.

It looks like the selection is the same for all of the promos, featuring a battery, charger, and a lot of core-type brushless power tools.

Everyone likes to say that these are free tool deals, that Lowe’s and Dewalt are giving them away. It’s really a “built your own combo kit” type of promo at a significant discount.

If you ask me, these look to be great deals, except for the lowest tier at least until they drop the price.

I think the 2-free tool deal is the sweet spot for most people.

Buy the 1-Free Tool Deal
Buy the 2-Free Tool Deal
Buy the 3-Free Tool Deal

Even though the deals’ end date is 3 months away, I have made 2 important observations in recent years.

First, the best deals sometimes sell out quickly. You’re not competing with other shoppers, you’re competing with shoppers and resellers that flip discounted tools on ebay and Amazon.

Since we’re still in October, there’s plenty of time for replenishment, and stores will likely get lots of inventory. I wouldn’t worry about anything selling out just yet.

Second, Lowe’s sometimes changes or ends deals without warning. Don’t take the 1/20/27 end date as a concrete promise.
